items.label: WUE metrics misrepresent local ecological impact
items.description: A situation that conflates operational cooling efficiency with the broader environmental health of local water resources. Encompasses: critiques of water usage metrics in data center regulation, arguments against using internal efficiency as a sustainability proxy. Excludes: broader debates on energy source carbon intensity or general economic cost-benefit analysis of AI infrastructure.

items.label: WUE metrics fail to measure sustainability
items.description: A situation that evaluates the technical limitations of Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) metrics regarding local environmental impact. Encompasses: critiques of standardized water accounting, arguments against water source neutrality, and assessments of aquifer depletion risks. Excludes: broader corporate ESG reporting strategies or non-technical water policy debates.
items.evidence: Industry standards from organizations like The Green Grid confirm that WUE does not differentiate between water sources or account for local water scarcity, rendering it ineffective as an indicator of aquifer sustainability.

items.label: Ineffective Data Center Tax Incentives
items.description: A situation that involves public subsidies for infrastructure projects failing to generate promised long-term employment. Encompasses: corporate welfare debates, economic impact assessments of tax breaks. Excludes: general industry growth trends or purely technical data center operations.
items.evidence: Data centers receive billions in tax breaks through state-level programs that often yield few permanent jobs, supporting the claim of subsidized expansion.

items.label: State legislative action refutes accountability claims
items.description: A situation that demonstrates active regulatory oversight of AI infrastructure through state-level mandates. Encompasses: environmental reporting requirements and large-load utility tariffs. Excludes: federal AI policy or voluntary industry self-regulation.
items.evidence: In 2025 alone, U.S. states introduced over 200 bills to mandate environmental reporting and establish 'large-load' utility tariffs, contradicting the claim that there is no accountability.
